text.p: Australia's state-owned telephone carrier Telstra Corp Ltd will to have to lose market share once the industry is deregulated, but it still expects to lift its business, a Telstra executive said on Friday.

Under Australia's deregulation of the telecommunications sector, which takes effect next Tuesday, there is no restriction on the number of carriers in the local market. At the moment there are two -- Telstra and Optus Communications Pty Ltd.
Telstra's director of regulatory affairs Graham Ward said the local telcoms market would grow through new product and services that come along with new players.

"I think the supply of telecommunications and informational services will become increasingly more important in the way we lead our lives and in turn could lead to a growth in the whole market," Ward told Reuters.

Telstra has a near stranglehold on Australia's A$5.0 billion dollar local call market, despite partial deregulation of the industry since 1992 which allowed the entry of Optus in the long distance market and mobile markets.
Ward said there was still growth in the local call market.
"There is still a lot of elasticity left in the Australian local call market, which has lower usage rates than many other countries, particularly the U.S.," Ward said.
But Telstra has to lose market share in the local call market if there is to be true competition in the Australian telecoms market, which is valued at about A$25 billion.
Over the past five years, Telstra market share of the overseas call market has fallen from 100 percent to about 69 percent of overseas market and about 75 percent of the long distance market.
Analysts expect Telstra to lose a similar amount in the local call market, but Ward would not comment on how much share Telstra would have in that market.

On Friday, the Business Review Weekly (BRW) magazine quoted Telstra chief executive Frank Blount as saying he would be happy if Telstra had a market share of between 50 and 60 percent in five years' time.
Analysts expect Telstra to focus on particular markets as it covered too broad a market.
"At the moment Telstra is addressing a market of nine million people and there no company that can have a focus on nine million customers," independent telecoms analyst Paul Buddie told Reuters.

Besides facing an increase in competition the government owned Telstra will also have to confront the rigours of the investment markets when it partially floats later this year with the sale of one third of the government's stake.
